To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) large differences were observed among common wheat cultivars and among cultivars and corresponding doubled-haplod lines derived by anther-culture for androgenic responses, (2) differences in response among cultivars and doubled haploids were not consistent with the hypothesis that anthers cultured in vitro constitute a general selective device, and (3) the environment of the anther-donor plants had a large influence on the androgenic response, and this influence was not consistent among cultivars

(1) large differences exist among wheat cultivars and doubledhaploids in anther callusing and plantlet regeneration frequency, and (2) the effects of environment on these processes vary with the cultivar and/or doubled-haploid.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic and physiological bases of the variation observed for anther culture response in wheat.
the development of an efficient system for the production of wheat doubled haploids.
developing a better understanding of the genetic and environmental effects on the androgenic process in wheat.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of environment on anther culture response in wheat are not consistent and are difficult to generalize.
the effects of cultivars and their corresponding doubled-haploidy lines, of environment, and of the interaction of cultivar and environment are all important factors in androgenic response.

anther culture responses are affected by a number of complex interactions of genotype and environment, but that these interactions do not necessarily lead to a general selection of the most responsive genotypes for doubled-haploid production.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the response of wheat anthers to culture varies greatly with genotype, genotype x environment, and environment itself, and that the anther culture response is not necessarily related to genotype per se.

the androgenic response in wheat appears to be a highly variable trait, with significant genetic effects and strong effects of environment, and that the response of anther culture is not necessarily superior to that of the corresponding cultivar.
androgenic response is affected by a complex interaction of factors including the genotype, its environment, and their interaction.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the effects of genotype and environment on androgenesis in wheat are complex, with the effects of genotype often overriding the effects of environment, and with the effects of environment being more important when the genotype is held constant.

the effects of cultivars on androgenic response are complex and that, in general, the use of anther culture to produce doubled-haploidy in wheat should be done with the cultivar of interest, not with a doubled-haploid derived from that cultivar, as the source of donor plants.

androgenesis is a complex trait, influenced by a large number of factors, including genotype, environment, and the interaction between them, and that the use of doubled-haploid populations in anther culture studies is likely to be useful for dissecting these factors.
